title: Pro Defensione Augustini Contra Cassiani Presbyteri Librum / Liber Contra Collatorem / S. PROSPERI AQUITANI DE GRATIA DEI ET LIBERO ARBITRIO a LIBER CONTRA COLLATOREM, ID EST, PRO DEFENSIONE S. AURELII AUGUSTINI, HIPPONENSIS EPISCOPI, CONTRA CASSIANI PRESBYTERI LIBRUM, QUI TITULO DE PROTECTIONE DEI PRÆNOTATUR
author: Prosperus Aquitanus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp831.tmp831.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Excutit duodecim definitiones Joannis Cassiani, de gratia et libero arbitrio. contentas collatione ipsius tertia decimi easque, una excepta prima, omnino a catholica veritate dissidere docet : demonstrans Augustini reprehensores, et van objicere et recta impugnare, et prava defendere, ipsisque Pelagianorum jam peremptorum armis intestinum bellum moventes, Scripturis divinis simul, et ecclesiasticis imperatoriisque constitutionibus rebellare.
passages.english: He examines twelve definitions of John Cassian concerning grace and free will, contained in his thirteenth Conference, and shows that, with the single exception of the first, they all depart entirely from catholic truth: demonstrating that Augustine's critics both raise empty objections and attack what is right and defend what is wrong, and that, stirring up a civil war with the very weapons of the Pelagians who have already been destroyed, they rebel at once against the divine Scriptures and against the decrees of the Church and of the emperors.
passages.notes: "van" read as "vana" (empty); "tertia decimi" read as "tertia decima" (thirteenth).

passages.original: Cassianus nec cum Pelagianis, nec cum Catholicis plene concordat: dum errando asserit alios per gratiam, alios per legem et naturam justificari. Definitio tertia Cassiani : Appetitum virtutum habere hominem a se ipso. Refellitur ex antea confessis in prima definitione.
passages.english: Cassian agrees fully neither with the Pelagians nor with the Catholics, since he wrongly asserts that some are justified through grace, others through the law and nature. Cassian's third definition: that man has the desire for the virtues from himself. It is refuted from what he had previously conceded in the first definition.

passages.original: Definitio quinta Cassiani : Simul suscipiendas esse sententia: contrarias; et illam quæ bonam voluntatem nasci ex gratia, et illam quæ ex bona voluntate gratiam pendere dicit. Opinio Cassiani catholicis perinde atque Pelagianis errorem affingit.
passages.english: Cassian's fifth definition: that contrary opinions are to be accepted together, both the one which says that good will is born from grace, and the one which says that grace depends on good will. Cassian's opinion imputes error to the Catholics just as much as to the Pelagians.

passages.original: Tu nos subdis duobus, et geminas, sicut intelligis, pravitates : dividendo damnas, miscendo justificas. Hac lege, m hac regula poteris praedicare, quod tam errent n qui dicunt, semper esse fallendum, quam qui definiunt numquam esse fallendum (Notatur 17 Collat. Cassiani, in qua docet quandoque esse licitum mentiri); sed ut in neutro peccetur, utrumque sectandum : ° quia nec semper declinanda falsitas, nec semper negligenda sit vertas. Fallit te prorsus opinio tua. De duobus malis unum fieri bonum non potest : unam virtutem duo vitia non gignunt : unum verum duo falsa non faciunt.
passages.english: You subject us to two, and, as you understand it, twin perversities: by dividing them you condemn, by mixing them you justify. By this law and this rule you will be able to preach that those who say one must always deceive err just as much as those who lay down that one must never deceive (Cassian's 17th Conference is meant, in which he teaches that it is sometimes permitted to lie); but that, so as to sin in neither, both are to be followed, because neither is falsehood always to be avoided nor truth always to be neglected. Your opinion deceives you completely. One good cannot be made out of two evils; two vices do not beget one virtue; two falsehoods do not make one truth.
passages.notes: Stray letters (m, n, °) omitted as footnote marks; "vertas" read as "veritas". The parenthesis is an editorial note in the printed text.

passages.original: » Et iterum cum de primi hominis scriberet lapsu : « Liberum enim, inquit, arbitrium olim ille perpessus, dum suis inconsultius utitur bonis, cadens in praevaricationis profunda demersus c est, et nihil quemadmodum exinde surgere posset, invenit; suaque in æternum libertate deceptus, d hujus ruinæ jacuisset oppressu, nisi eum post Christi pro sua gratia e relevasset adventus. » Erraverunt ORIENTALES EPISCOPI, in quorum judicio Pelagius, eos qui dicunt gratiam Dei secundum merita nostra dari, ut catholicus posset videri, auathematizare compulsus est (Vide lib. de Gestis Pelagii c. XIV, 33-55). Erraverunt f AFRICANA episcoporum CONCILI, quae decretis suis constituerunt, utrumque Dei donum esse, et scire quid facere debeamus, et diligere ut faciamus : ut ædificante charitate, scientia non possit inflare, quia sicut de Deo scriplum est, g Qui docet hominem scientiam (Ps.
passages.english: And again, when he was writing about the fall of the first man, he said: "For he, having once undergone [the experience of] free choice, while he used his own goods too heedlessly, fell and was sunk into the depths of transgression, and found no way by which he could rise from there; and, deceived by his own freedom for ever, he would have lain crushed under this ruin, had not the coming of Christ afterwards raised him up by his grace." The EASTERN BISHOPS erred, in whose judgment Pelagius was compelled to anathematize those who say that the grace of God is given according to our merits, so that he might appear catholic (see the book On the Proceedings of Pelagius, ch. 14, 33-55). The COUNCILS of the AFRICAN bishops erred, which established by their decrees that both are a gift of God, both to know what we ought to do and to love so that we do it, so that, with charity building up, knowledge cannot puff up; because, just as it is written of God, He who teaches man knowledge (Ps.
passages.notes: Scattered letters (c, d, e, f, g) are footnote marks and are omitted. "auathematizare" read as "anathematizare"; "scriplum" as "scriptum"; "CONCILI" taken as "concilia". "pro sua gratia" may refer to Christ's grace ("by his grace"). The passage breaks off mid-reference; the quotation continues in the following text.

passages.original: Cum ea quæstio, quæ est de sanctarum origine volun- talum, contra Pelagianos clare definila sit; male Cassianus, errantium arma colligens, contendit
passages.english: Since the question concerning the origin of holy wills has been clearly defined against the Pelagians, Cassian, gathering up the weapons of those in error, wrongly contends
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence (a chapter heading); the object of "contends" is missing.

passages.original: Primus homo, cieaMus absque vitio, et potens in bono perseverare si vellet, libero arbitrio discessit a bono : in quo post peccatum nihil remansit, nisi quod ad temporalem pertinet vitam. In quam profundum malum tota humana natura demersa sit illius prævaricatione. Definitio septima Cassiani : Adamum
passages.english: The first man, created without fault and able to persevere in good if he wished, departed from good by free will; in him after the sin nothing remained except what pertains to temporal life. Into how deep an evil the whole of human nature was plunged by his transgression. Cassian's seventh definition: that Adam
passages.notes: "cieaMus" read as "creatus". The text breaks off mid-sentence.

VII in Lucæ c. xv). » Quod ita non falso dixit beatus Ambrosius, sicut non falso ipsa Veritas ait,f Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvare quod perierat (Luc. XIX, 10). Naturæ enim humanæ, in illa universalis prævaricationis ruina, nee substantia I erepta est nec voluntas; sed lumen decusque virtutum, quibus fraude invidentis exuta est Perditis autem per quæ ad æternam atque inamissibilem corporis k animique ineorruplionem poterat pervenire, quid ei remansit, nisi quod ad tempora)em pertinet vitum, quae tota est damnationis et poenae ?
passages.english: remained good, he departed from the law set before him; nor did he fear the penalty of death announced to him, deserting God and following the devil, rebellious to the Lord his preserver and obedient to the enemy his destroyer. "Adam existed, then, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished (Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, ch. 15)." Blessed Ambrose said this no more falsely than the Truth itself said, "The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished" (Luke 19:10). For in that ruin of universal transgression neither its substance nor its will was taken from human nature, but the light and adornment of the virtues, of which it was stripped by the deceit of the envious one. But once the things were lost through which it could have attained the eternal and unlosable incorruption of body and soul, what remained to it except what pertains to temporal life, which is wholly a life of damnation and punishment?
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence ("by which free will, as long as he wished, he remained good"). Scanning errors corrected (supplicium, formidavit, omnes, ineorruplionem, vitam); stray marks omitted.

passages.original: Liberum arbitrium nec voluntatem boni, nec possibilitatem habere, nisi per gratiam. Cur homini imperentur ea quorum facultatem non invenit in sua natura. Definitio octava Cassiani : Naturæ humanæ non id solum ascribendum quod malum est. Merita hominum nulla nisi ex gratia.
passages.english: That free will has neither the will for good nor the ability for it except through grace. Why things are commanded of man the capacity for which he does not find in his own nature. Cassian's eighth definition: that not only what is evil is to be ascribed to human nature. That men have no merits except from grace.

passages.original: 13, cap. 12): Unde cavendum nobis est, ne ita b ad Deum omnia sanctorum merita referamus, ut Mihil nisi id quod malum atque perversum est humanæ ascribamus naturæ. Quid evidentius, quid expressius secundum Pelagii Coelestiique commentum ab ullo c eorum discipulo ponit definiri ? IN! dicunt, Gratiam Dei secundum merita nostra dari; d et iidem dicunt, Gratiam Dei non ad singulos actus dari: hic intra unam sententiam blasphemiam utramque conclusit dicens, Cavendum nobis esse, ne ita ad Deum omnia sanctorum merita referamus, ut nihil niti quod malum atque perversum est humana ascribamus naturæ.
passages.english: 13, ch. 12): "Hence we must beware lest we so refer all the merits of the saints to God that we ascribe nothing to human nature except what is evil and perverse." What could be defined more evidently, what more expressly, in accordance with the invention of Pelagius and Caelestius, by any of their disciples? They say that the grace of God is given according to our merits; and the same men say that the grace of God is not given for individual acts. This man has enclosed both blasphemies within a single sentence, saying that we must beware lest we so refer all the merits of the saints to God that we ascribe nothing to human nature except what is evil and perverse.
passages.notes: Begins mid-citation (Cassian, Conference 13, ch. 12). Scanning errors corrected: "Mihil" = nihil, "niti" = nisi, "ponit" taken as potuit, "IN!" taken as Illi ("They"). Footnote letters omitted.

passages.original: Definitio nona Cassiani: Omni animæ inesse naturaliter virtutum semina, a Creatore inserta. Refellitur, quia peccatum originale evertit. Virtutes in impiis veras non esse, sed omnia opera eorum immunda. Virtutum sive meritorum principia nulla in nobis ante gratiam.
passages.english: Cassian's ninth definition: that in every soul there are naturally present seeds of the virtues, implanted by the Creator. It is refuted, because it overturns original sin. That virtues in the ungodly are not true, but all their works are unclean. That there are no beginnings of virtues or merits in us before grace.

passages.original: Cassianus liberi arbitrii vigorem demonstrare aggressus. Definitio decima Cassiani: Job suis viribus vicisse diabolum, non auxilio grative : nisi quatenus Deus non majorem tentatori dedit potestatem, quam illi noverat inesse virtutem. Cassiani fraus : catholicam sententiam de gratia in disputationis principio prædicat, et eamdem postea impugnat.
passages.english: Cassian undertakes to demonstrate the strength of free will. Cassian's tenth definition: that Job conquered the devil by his own strength, not by the help of grace, except insofar as God did not give the tempter greater power than He knew Job had virtue. Cassian's deceit: he proclaims the catholic doctrine of grace at the beginning of the discussion and afterwards attacks it.

passages.original: Cassianus inconvenientia miscere conatur, et fideles in duo genera dividit, quibus contraria accommodet. Definitio duod cimu Cassiani : Deum in salutis negotio aliis esse salvatorem. aliis susceptorem tantum. Contra probat S. Prosper. Christum omnium qui salvantur esse salvatorem. Placita Cassiani de gratia et libero arbitrio horrescunt evangelicæ apostolicæque doctrinæ discipuli.
passages.english: Cassian tries to mix incompatible things, and divides the faithful into two kinds, to which he may apply contrary [doctrines]. Twelfth definition of Cassian: that in the business of salvation God is the saviour of some, but of others only the receiver. Against this Saint Prosper proves that Christ is the saviour of all who are saved. The disciples of the gospel and apostolic teaching shudder at Cassian's opinions on grace and free will.
passages.notes: This appears to be a chapter summary (capitulum) added by the editor rather than Prosper's own text. 'duod cimu' read as 'duodecima' (twelfth). 'susceptorem' (receiver, one who takes up) contrasts with 'salvatorem': God merely receives those who come of their own accord, rather than saving them.

Cœlestini ad Gal. ep.), sanctæ recordationis virum, pro vita sua atque pro meritis, in nostra semper communione habuimus; nec umquam hunc s nistræ suspicionis saltem rnmor aspersit, quem tantæ scientic olim fuisse meminimus, ut inter magistros optimos etiam a meis semper i decessorihus haberetur.
passages.english: [This was] when, having taken up the case of those who consulted him, and having praised the piety of the books which displeased those in error, he made known in holy words what ought to be thought about their authority. He declared plainly how much the novelty of this presumption displeased him, by which certain people dared to rise up insolently against the ancient teachers and to clamour against the preaching of the truth with unruly slander: "Augustine, a man of holy memory," he said (Letter of Celestine to the Gallic bishops), "we have always held in our communion because of his life and his merits; nor did even a rumour of sinister suspicion ever sprinkle him. We remember that he was once of such great knowledge that he was always counted among the best teachers even by my predecessors."
passages.notes: The subject 'he' is Pope Celestine I (named as 'this man' in the preceding context). Scanning errors corrected silently: 'librorum', 'errantibus', 'eloquio', 'sibi', 'displiceret', 'veritatis', 'sinistræ rumor', 'scientiæ', 'decessoribus'; stray letters (I, f, h, s, i) treated as footnote marks.
